Neonates of the Golden cownose ray emerge from the mother with a disc width at birth of approximately 40 centimeters [Lb = approximately 40 centimeters], a value consistent with the range of 38 to 45 cm reported in earlier accounts for this species. This initial size is relatively modest compared to the dimensions the animal will eventually attain, setting the stage for a prolonged growth trajectory through the juvenile and sub-adult stages. Pups are fully independent upon parturition and immediately begin exogenous feeding, actively foraging for benthic invertebrates in shallow coastal waters. The disc width at birth (40 centimeters) [Lb = 40 centimeters] likely reflects a compromise between the constraints of gestation within the mother and the need for the neonate to be sufficiently large to avoid predation and capture prey effectively. Newly born individuals display the characteristic wing-like pectoral fins and the pronounced, somewhat bulbous forehead that gives the cownose ray its common name. The size of the offspring at birth has implications for early survival rates and for the subsequent timing of life history events such as the onset of gonadal activity and eventual recruitment into the breeding population.

Reproductive output in this myliobatid ray is modest when compared with many teleost fishes, a common pattern among elasmobranchs that invest heavily in individual offspring. The maximum reproductive rate has been quantified as approximately one pup every 365 days [Ri = approximately one pup every 365 days] under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C]. This low fecundity, with females typically producing a single litter each year, highlights the vulnerability of the species to overexploitation. The gestation period requires substantial energetic investment from the gravid female, who must nourish the developing embryos through a yolk-dependent placenta. Following parturition, a period of reproductive quiescence may ensue before the female is ready for a subsequent mating event, further limiting the annual recruitment potential. The disc width at birth (40 cm) [Lb = 40 cm] remains an important parameter for population models, as it defines the starting point for the growth curve. Emigration and immigration patterns in coastal nursery grounds may also be influenced by the size of the neonate at emergence.

Sexual maturation in the Golden cownose ray is attained when individuals reach a disc width at puberty of roughly 70 centimeters [Lp = roughly 70 centimeters], a milestone that marks the transition from a growing juvenile to a reproductively viable adult capable of participating in annual breeding aggregations. This size threshold is not reached until several years after birth, given the species' relatively slow somatic growth rate. The age at birth itself is known to be approximately 366 days [ab = approximately 366 days], or roughly 12 months, when the embryos are incubated at 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C]. The protracted gestation and late age at maturity together produce a generation time that is characteristic of slow life-history strategists among the batoids. Females likely store sperm after copulation, using clasper-mediated insemination, allowing them to fertilize successive clutches without repeated mating. The attainment of 70 centimeters [Lp = 70 centimeters] in disc width signals the onset of ovarian maturation and the individual's entry into the pool of sexually mature adults, a stage accompanied by changes in migratory behavior and habitat use in many myliobatid species.

Field records and laboratory studies suggest that the ultimate disc width, or the maximum size attained by adults, approaches 90 centimeters [Li = 90 centimeters] in large, presumably old individuals. This asymptotic size represents the upper bound of the growth curve and is comparable to values reported for the congeneric Atlantic cownose ray, Rhinoptera bonasus, from the western Atlantic. Attaining this size requires many years of sustained feeding and growth. The maximum lifespan of the species, based on comparisons with its close relative R. bonasus, is estimated at 26 years [am = 26 years] under environmental conditions averaging 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C]. This extended longevity is consistent with the general pattern in elasmobranchs, where late maturity and low fecundity are balanced by high adult survival rates. Individuals that survive the early juvenile bottlenecks can persist for decades, contributing to the population over many successive breeding seasons. The large ultimate disc width (90 centimeters) [Li = 90 centimeters] likely confers advantages in predator avoidance and in the ability to handle larger, more energetically profitable prey items such as bivalves and crustaceans.

From a comparative life-history perspective, the Golden cownose ray exhibits a notably slow pace of life, even among myliobatid rays. The age at birth of about 366 days [ab = about 366 days] is a direct consequence of the lengthy gestation demanded by the production of a single, well-develop at a temperature of 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C]ed pup. Following birth, the juvenile phase extends over several years before the disc width at puberty of 70 centimeters [Lp = 70 centimeters] is finally achieved. Once mature, the annual production of one pup per year [Ri = one pup per year] at 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C] yields a lifetime reproductive output that, though low on an annual basis, accumulates over a maximum lifespan of 26 years [am = 26 years] to produce a meaningful number of offspring. The ultimate disc width of 90 centimeters [Li = 90 centimeters] represents the culmination of this slow growth trajectory. Physiological senescence likely occurs gradually in the oldest age classes, but the combination of delayed maturity, low fecundity, and long life makes the species particularly sensitive to increases in juvenile or adult mortality from fishing pressure or habitat degradation.
